speaker: Rob
text: [warmly] Hello, and welcome. This is One "Zì" at a Time, the show where we learn to read Chinese starting from absolute zero, one character at a time. I'm Rob, and with me is my co-host, Sunshine.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [warmly] Hi, Rob. Hi, everyone. I'm so happy to be here.

speaker: Rob
text: And I'm happy you said yes.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [chuckles] Of course I did! This is a good idea. So, this whole show is Rob's. He came to me with a different way of teaching Chinese and asked if I'd help him build it. [curious] But Rob, I don't think I ever heard the whole story. How did you come up with this?

speaker: Rob
text: [thoughtfully] Well... [chuckles] that's a story for another episode. Right now I'd rather just show you. The idea is simple. We go one character at a time, starting from zero.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [playfully] Oh, so the history is a mystery, eh? Fine, I'll allow it. So one at a time from zero? [curious] And we'll never have to read or repeat something we haven't covered yet, right?

speaker: Rob
text: Right. Every sentence has exactly one character you don't already know.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [warmly] I love that. So, how is each episode going to work?

speaker: Rob
text: [brightly] Okay. In every episode, Sunshine, you'll introduce one new character, and we'll talk about what it looks like and where it comes from. Then you'll tell us about any new words it unlocks. And then you'll read us a good number of sentences, and I'll do my best to translate them, before we move on to the next character. We'll do that a few times each episode.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [excited] One character, the words it unlocks, and lots of sentences. I like it. And you get to be the one who has to guess what everything means.

speaker: Rob
text: [dryly] I'm going to be humbled, aren't I.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] A little. [excited] I'm ready to try it. Shall we start?

speaker: Rob
text: [grins] [brightly] Yeah. Let's get started!

speaker: Rob
text: [sheepishly] Okay. So. About what I said earlier. One character at a time, nothing you haven't covered yet. [hesitates] We need to make an exception.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] Rob! You can't do that! [exasperated] It's the very first episode, and you're already breaking the entire premise of the show!

speaker: Rob
text: [urgently] I know! But these words don't mean anything! They're just noises you make at the end of a sentence! They're more of a feeling than anything!

speaker: Sunshine
text: [sighs] Do they have a character that's drawn?

speaker: Rob
text: Yes.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [reluctantly] And do they need to be read?

speaker: Rob
text: [sheepishly] ...Um... Yes.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [defeated] Ugh. This gives me the ick. Okay, how many are there?

speaker: Rob
text: [brightly] Four. Think of it as character zero. A warm-up.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] I think you mean Characters zero. There's more than one, remember?

speaker: Rob
text: [embarrassed] Oh, yeah... right...

speaker: Sunshine
text: [warmly] Okay, let me get a look at them. These four are... well, they're sentence-ending particles. They don't have a meaning of their own, they add a mood. All four are neutral tone, so they're light and quick, and they tuck in right at the end of a sentence. And look, they all start with the same piece.

speaker: Rob
text: [curious] The little square box on the left? It looks like an open mouth.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Exactly. That's the mouth radical. It makes sense, since these are all sounds you make with your mouth. The right side is a hint at the sound.

speaker: Rob
text: Because humans make sounds with mouths, right?

speaker: Sunshine
text: [brightly] That's what I've been told! Okay, so, if you're going to break a rule by introducing four characters at once, I'm going to cheat too and use some sentences so the listeners can get a feel for what these words sound like.

speaker: Rob
text: That sounds fair...

speaker: Sunshine
text: First, "啊". It adds warmth or surprise, like an extra little "oh!" on the end. Listen.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 好啊！

speaker: Rob
text: Okay, so that definitely sounds surprised...

speaker: Sunshine
text: Next, "呢". It turns a sentence into a gentle follow-up question, like "and what about...?"

speaker: Sunshine
text: 你呢？

speaker: Rob
text: Sounds soft and gentle really... I guess asking what your choice would be?

speaker: Sunshine
text: Pretty much, yeah. The third, "呀". It makes a greeting or a call sound friendly. The right side here is the character for tooth.

speaker: Rob
text: [amused] A mouth with a tooth in it. Okay, that's a good picture.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] Now listen.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 你好呀！

speaker: Rob
text: Definitely showing a lot of friendliness in that one.

speaker: Sunshine
text: And last, "吧". It softens a suggestion, like "let's" or "how about."

speaker: Sunshine
text: 我们走吧。

speaker: Rob
text: It almost sounds like a command, but maybe a little less forceful. Like "Let's go."

speaker: Rob
text: [brightly] See, that wasn't so bad! We've already finished character zero!

speaker: Sunshine
text: [warmly] I think you mean characters zero, plural. But yeah, that's four little feelings that don't mean anything on their own.

speaker: Rob
text: [dryly] And now we can go back to doing this properly.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [teasing] Are you sure there won't be any more exceptions?

speaker: Rob
text: [dryly] Yeah I'm positive. Mostly. Okay, let's move on to character one, singular!

speaker: Sunshine
text: It better be.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [brightly] Okay! Character number one. "Shì." Fourth tone, the falling one. Say it like you're completely sure of yourself.

speaker: Rob
text: [dryly] Character one. Singular. What's it mean?

speaker: Sunshine
text: It means "to be." Is, are, am.

speaker: Rob
text: All three?

speaker: Sunshine
text: All three. I am, you are, he is, they are. Same character every time. It never changes.

speaker: Rob
text: [suspicious] Nothing on the end? No different form for "I" or "they"? No past tense version? [slowly] English has am, is, are, was, were, been, being. But Chinese hands you one word and walks off?

speaker: Sunshine
text: Exactly. If you want to show WHEN something happened, other words in the sentence do that. This one just stays the same.

speaker: Rob
text: [thoughtfully] I don't trust it. Okay, I'm looking at it on the screen. There's a little box at the top with a line across the middle, like a window. And underneath there's... a lot to look at.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Well, the box on top is the sun. The part underneath is related to "correct," or "straight."

speaker: Rob
text: The sun... on top of "correct."

speaker: Sunshine
text: Here's an old folk history trick. It's like, the sun is straight overhead at noon, and nothing is in doubt. "That's right. It is so." And that's the other meaning. It can also mean "yes," or "that's right." Someone asks you something, and you can answer with just this.

speaker: Rob
text: So it's "to be" and it's "yes." For a first character, that's a pretty good deal.

speaker: Sunshine
text: That's why it goes first. Nothing else is unlocked yet, so today's whole word list is just "Shì," on its own.

speaker: Rob
text: One character, one word. Character one, singular, and it actually stayed singular. [warmly] I'm proud of us.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] Don't get used to it.

speaker: Rob
text: Okay, so, I should explain something first. We're going to start reading out example sentences now. These come from a document I made with LOTS of example sentences. I'll try to make these available, but haven't figured out how yet.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [brightly] Sure, Rob. But I DO have the sentences, so we can just jump right in.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [brightly] These first three are going to look almost identical on the page, so I'll read them back to back.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 1.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 是。

speaker: Sunshine
text: That's a plain statement. "Yes." Or "It is." Just calm and flat.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 2.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 是？

speaker: Sunshine
text: [curious] Now my voice goes up. "Yes?" "Is it?"

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 3.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 是！

speaker: Sunshine
text: [excitedly] And that's "Yes!" Like you really mean it.

speaker: Rob
text: [dryly] So that's three sentences, one character, and the only thing that changed was the punctuation.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] Exactly. The punctuation does all the work.

speaker: Rob
text: Which is great for me, because the punctuation is the one part I can actually read.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 4.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 是啊！

speaker: Rob
text: Okay, that's our word plus the warm tone. So something like "Oh, yes!" or "It sure is!"

speaker: Sunshine
text: [warmly] Yep, "It sure is!" Like when a friend says "Nice weather today," and you agree with them.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 5.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 是呀！

speaker: Rob
text: That sounded a lot like the last one, just a little brighter. The cheerful, surprised one? "Oh, yes!"

speaker: Sunshine
text: Right. It's basically the same as Sentence 4, just a bit more bouncy. You hear it a lot from kids, and from me.

speaker: Rob
text: [dryly] I've noticed.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 6.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 是吧？

speaker: Rob
text: [thoughtfully] That's the checking one, with a question mark. So: "Right?" "It is, isn't it?"

speaker: Sunshine
text: Perfect. You're not totally sure, so you want the other person to agree with you.

speaker: Rob
text: I'll be using that one a lot.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 8.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 是呢。

speaker: Rob
text: Hm. My notes say that last one is the gentle question, "what about...?" But this ends with a period. So, "Is it... what about it"? I'm not getting anywhere with that.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] Fair, it's a tricky one. With a period, it's not really a question. It's a soft agreement, like you're nodding along. "Yeah, it is."

speaker: Rob
text: So it's a quieter version of Sentence 4.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Yes! Sentence 4 is "It sure is!" and this one is "Mm, it is."

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 14.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 是啊，是吧？

speaker: Rob
text: Two pieces. The first is the warm "Oh, yes," and the second is the checking one. So: "Oh yes, it is, right?"

speaker: Sunshine
text: [warmly] That's it. You agree, and then you check that they agree with you too.

speaker: Rob
text: [dryly] Agreeing with myself and then asking for confirmation. Sounds like me in a meeting.

speaker: Rob
text: Ok, so, do we need to review what we learned?

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] Well, there's not really that much to review! I think we can just move on to our second character.

speaker: Rob
text: Yeah, I think so too.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [warmly] Good, because our next character is super important.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [excitedly] Character number two is "Bù." Fourth tone, the falling one. It means "not," or just "no." This is the super important part: it's the other half of yes and no.

speaker: Rob
text: This used to be my daughter's favorite word. It still is, but it used to be, too. [dryly] So we learned yes, and now we're learning no. Seems like a very balanced show, we're making here.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] Exactly. Put the two together and you can ask real questions and answer them. But first, let's look at it.

speaker: Rob
text: [thoughtfully] Okay. There's a flat line across the top and a stroke dropping down from the middle. Then two little strokes kick out underneath, one left, one right. It looks like a tiny tree. Or a coat rack.

speaker: Sunshine
text: A tree is good! Some people see a bird with its wings spread out. Here's a memory trick. Imagine a bird flying up and hitting something flat above it, like a ceiling. It can't get through. So: no. Not.

speaker: Rob
text: Denied, rejected, no way José. I can remember that.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Good. "Bù" works on its own. If someone asks you something, you can just answer "Bù." No. Or you put it in front of another word to make that word negative.

speaker: Sunshine
text: That brings us to our first compound word: 不是.

speaker: Rob
text: So the pieces are "not," plus the one we just did, "is."

speaker: Sunshine
text: Right. "Not" plus "is."

speaker: Rob
text: [curious] So literally, "not is", but more like "It's not like that."

speaker: Sunshine
text: [warmly] Yes! 不是 means "is not," or as an answer, just "no." If someone asks whether this is your coffee and it isn't, you say 不是.

speaker: Rob
text: Fine, but I'm going to hear "not is" in my head forever.

speaker: Sunshine
text: That's okay. One small sound thing: "Bù" is a falling tone, but when it comes right before another falling tone, like it does here, it rises instead. So in 不是 the first part goes up and the second part comes down.

speaker: Rob
text: [dryly] So the word for "no" doesn't always follow its own rules. I'm kind of not at all surprised by this, really.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] Very wise. Next word: 是不是.

speaker: Rob
text: Okay, so that's "is," then "not," then "is" again. Is, not, is. [thoughtfully] Is... not... is. It sounds like someone who can't make up their mind.

speaker: Sunshine
text: That's actually really close! It means "is it, or is it not?" You use it to ask "is this true?" Basically, yes or no.

speaker: Rob
text: Nailed it.

speaker: Sunshine
text: You were right by accident. But it counts. Okay, the last one is a little sneaky. 不是.

speaker: Rob
text: [flatly] You already did that one.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] It's the same characters, yes. But when you say the second part light and soft, it means something else: "fault," or "blame." Like, "it's my fault."

speaker: Rob
text: [incredulous] Is this a common use?

speaker: Sunshine
text: Honestly, not really. You'll see the "is not" one a hundred times before you see this one.

speaker: Rob
text: [dryly] So not terribly useful for us, then. So that's four words. And now my daughter will know how to reply in Chinese when I ask her to do something.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [warmly] She can also ask yes-or-no questions, you know. That's kind of a big deal.

speaker: Rob
text: [flatly] Yeah... but she won't.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Time for sentences. Let's start with three quick ones. It's the same word every time, and only the little tone word on the end changes. Sentence 3.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 不是啊！

speaker: Rob
text: "No, it's not!" With some feeling behind it.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Yes, warm and emphatic.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 4.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 不是吧？

speaker: Rob
text: That's the "let's" or "right?" word, plus a question mark. So it's "It's not... right?" Someone who doesn't quite believe it.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] Exactly. "No way. Really?"

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 5.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 不是呀！

speaker: Rob
text: The cheerful, surprised "oh." So: "Oh, no it's not!" Correcting somebody, but nicely.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [excitedly] Three moods from one word! Okay, Rob, have you ever walked through a crowded market where all the sellers are shouting at you, trying to get your attention, to buy stuff?

speaker: Rob
text: [dryly] Every vacation I've ever taken. I don't understand a word of it, so I just keep waving and walking.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] Then you already know the next three. Sentence 7.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 不，不是。

speaker: Rob
text: "No, it's not." That's the first seller, and I'm still being polite. I even finished my sentence with a period.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 9.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 不,不,不

speaker: Rob
text: "No, no, no." No period this time. [rushed] I'm not finishing sentences anymore, I'm just walking.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughing] And waving your hand, like you're brushing off a fly. And...

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 12.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 不是，不是！

speaker: Rob
text: "No, it's not, it's not!" With an exclamation point. This guy has followed me past three stalls already!

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] Now you sound annoyed, and that's exactly right. The last two go together: one question, two possible answers. Away from the crowded market, just with friends.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 13.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 是不是？是！

speaker: Rob
text: "Is it or isn't it? It is!" Yes or no, and the answer is yes.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [warmly] Right. And to answer, you just pick one half of the question. Here's the other half.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 19.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 是不是？不是。

speaker: Rob
text: "Is it? It's not." Same question, but this time the answer is no. The period here means it's calmer, right?

speaker: Sunshine
text: That's right. [laughs] There's no reason to get mad when talking with friends or family.

speaker: Rob
text: I think my daughter didn't get the memo.

speaker: Rob
text: Okay, we should review this one. Quick recap?

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sure. Our second character was "Bù." Fourth tone, and it means "not" or "no."

speaker: Rob
text: And it gave us two words that matter. "Is not," and "is it or isn't it," for asking yes-or-no questions.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [warmly] And the fourth one, the "fault" word, is the one you can safely forget for now.

speaker: Rob
text: [dryly] Already forgotten. And in some other sentences, one little sound at the end changed the mood three different ways.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] And you survived again. You're making a habit of this.

speaker: Rob
text: Barely. But now I can say no, and mean it.

speaker: Rob
text: I am wondering what the next one might be.

speaker: Sunshine
text: I am sure you are. I think you'll find this one useful. I know it's a great start to sentences.

speaker: Rob
text: [dryly] I... don't get it.

speaker: Sunshine
text: I can tell. [laughs] Notice how every sentence we just said started with the same word?

speaker: Rob
text: [slowly] Wait... the word is "I"?

speaker: Sunshine
text: [excitedly] Yeah! Character number three is "Wǒ." Third tone, the dipping one. It means "I," "me," and "my."

speaker: Rob
text: So one character covers "I," "me," and "my"? I don't have to figure out which form I need?

speaker: Sunshine
text: No choosing. Same character, whatever job it's doing. The rest of the sentence tells you what it means.

speaker: Rob
text: [thoughtfully] That's a relief. Okay, the shape. There's a hand on the left, reaching out. And on the right, something like a spear.

speaker: Sunshine
text: The right side really is an old weapon, a spear with a blade on it. Some say it's a person holding a spear, saying "This is mine. I'm me."

speaker: Rob
text: A guy defending himself with a spear. [dryly] Very confident for a word that just means "me."

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] It's easy to remember, at least. And like our first character, there are no new compound words today. Just "Wǒ," on its own.

speaker: Rob
text: Three characters in, and I can finally start talking about myself!

speaker: Sunshine
text: [warmly] Everyone's favorite topic.

speaker: Rob
text: Ok. Sentence time. Let's use this.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 1.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 是我！

speaker: Rob
text: [dryly] Literally, "is I," with an exclamation mark. Which we can tidy up into "It's me!"

speaker: Sunshine
text: [warmly] Yes! Like when someone knocks and you call out from the hallway.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 2.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 我是。

speaker: Rob
text: Same two pieces, flipped around. "I is." Once I've apologized to my English teacher, that's "I am."

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] Right. 是 never changes, so there's no am, is or are. The word order does all the work.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 4.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 我不是。

speaker: Rob
text: And now "not" is squeezed in front of "is." "I not is." So: "I'm not."

speaker: Sunshine
text: Perfect. 不 always goes right in front of 是. Now, picture a broken lamp on the floor. Someone is standing right next to it.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 3.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 不是我。。。

speaker: Rob
text: [thoughtfully] "Not is me." So, "Not me..." But those three dots are doing a lot of work. That's a person backing slowly toward the door.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] Very guilty! The voice just fades away. Now it's the same idea, but this time you really didn't do it.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 12.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 不是我呀！

speaker: Rob
text: That's the cheerful tone word on the end, the surprised "oh!" So: "Oh, it's not me!" Less lamp-breaker, more someone who just walked in with groceries.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [excitedly] Exactly! Bright and surprised. The same three characters give you a completely different person. Okay, the next two come as a pair.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 13.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 是不是我？

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 14.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 我是不是？

speaker: Rob
text: Same three pieces, and both are questions. The first starts with "is": "Is, not is, me?" That means "Is it me?" The second starts with "I": "I is, not is?" That's "Am I?"

speaker: Sunshine
text: [warmly] Yes! That 是不是 in the middle is the "is it or isn't it" question we met earlier. Put 我 at the end and you're asking "Is it me?" Put it at the front and you're asking about yourself: "Am I, or am I not?"

speaker: Rob
text: [dryly] So nothing gets added or taken away. You just shuffle the order and end up asking something else entirely.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [laughs] That's Chinese! Last one. Imagine someone asks for a volunteer.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Sentence 17.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 是我，是我！

speaker: Rob
text: "It's me, it's me!" Hand straight up, already half out of the chair.

speaker: Sunshine
text: [excitedly] Yeah! Say it twice, and everyone knows you really mean it.

speaker: Sunshine
text: Ok, let's repeat a few of them and see if you can remember them all.

speaker: Sunshine
text: 我是。

speaker: Sunshine
text: 不是我。。。

speaker: Sunshine
text: 我不是。

speaker: Sunshine
text: 不是我呀！

speaker: Sunshine
text: 是不是我？

speaker: Sunshine
text: 我是不是？

speaker: Rob
text: If you understood all that, I think we're ready to move on!
